title: Fallback lattice policy for latency and capacity coordination
creator: Ravi Patel
description: Problem: We currently rely on simple region-first routing with hard geo-pinning and standalone circuit breakers. During cross-region capacity stress this leads to abrupt failovers, cache churn (large KV cache misses), and repeated client retries that blow SLOs in downstream systems. We need a coordinated, multi-signal fallback lattice that balances per-region latency SLOs, remaining error budget, and short-term capacity forecasts to steer traffic gracefully.
proposal: Introduce a 'fallback lattice' policy: a cascaded policy graph that evaluates (1) region-local SLO health (burn rate, p99 latency), (2) capacity credit (token-bucket-derived short-term capacity budget), (3) KV cache affinity score, and (4) cost/variant preference. At each decision step the lattice emits an ordered list of candidate endpoints with weights and a 'degrade level' (none, soft-shed, hard-shed). Key behaviors: - Latency-first rejection: if local p99 > target AND burn rate > threshold, mark region as soft-shed candidate. - Capacity credits: regions consume credits for hedged calls; when credits low, reduce weight. - KV affinity: prefer endpoints with cached context for identical client prefixes to avoid cold-KV penalties. - Circuit breakers: open when error rate or queue length crosses configured hysteresis windows; close only after stable window. - Lattice mapping: fallback not binary; route percentage gradually from 0% to 100% over a grace window to avoid thundering herd.
design_decisions: - Use single unified signal store (time-series + short-term forecast) rather than ad-hoc heuristics to keep decision deterministic. - Soft-shed vs hard-shed: soft-shed substitutes a cheaper model variant or adds tokenized latency budget; hard-shed returns explicit 503s for non-critical clients. - Prefer steering heuristics as config-first (JSON rules) with server-side evaluation to enable rapid experiments. - Keep KV affinity as a soft boost rather than hard pin so we can maintain capacity elasticity.
rollout_plan: 1) Implement lattice evaluator and simulator in routing service; unit test with synthetic traces. 2) Dry-run mode in prod returning decisions in X-Response header for 48h and compare to current router. 3) Canary steer for 5% traffic for low-risk customers with canary model variants. 4) Gradual expansion by region and customer tier with automated kill-switch if SLO regressions detected. 5) Full rollout with opt-in enterprise control in Redwood Console.
metrics_to_monitor:
- p50/p95/p99 latency per region and overall
- error budget burn rate per region
- circuit breaker open counts and durations
- KV cache hit ratio and cold-start latencies
- folded soft-shed percentage and hard-shed 503 rate
- downstream retry amplification (client retry loops)
- synthetic canary latency/accuracy comparisons
testing_plan: - Simulator: replay 7-day production traffic with induced regional outages and autoscaler lag to validate decisions. - Chaos: controlled fail region (simulated 30s and 5m outages) and verify lattice migrates traffic without p99 spikes > 10%. - Load tests: exercise token-bucket credit exhaustion scenarios and verify gradual shedding. - Integration tests: ensure headers and tracing propagate steering decisions for observability. - Postmortem runbook updated with lattice-specific checks.
acceptance_criteria: Baseline: simulator shows <10% increase in global p99 vs current router for benign runs
Under regional partial outage: global p99 increases by <20% while degraded clients see documented 503 fallback behavior
Circuit breakers engage and recover without oscillation during 5m autoscaler lag scenario
KV affinity reduces cold-KV misses by at least 15% for pinned prefixes in canary region
Dry-run logs show 0 unexpected client-facing differences for enterprise customers in first 48h
